id: In Memoriam A. H. H. OBIIT MDCCCXXXIII: 124

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That which we dare invoke to bless; Our dearest faith; our ghastliest doubt; He, They, One, All; within, without; The Power in darkness whom we guess; I found Him not in world or sun, Or eagle's wing, or insect's eye; Nor thro' the questions men may try, The petty cobwebs we have spun: If e'er when faith had fall'n asleep, I heard a voice, "Believe no more," And heard an ever-breaking shore That tumbled in the Godless deep, A warmth within the breast would melt The freezing reason's colder part, And like a man in wrath the heart Stood up and answer'd, "I have felt." No, like a child in doubt and fear: But that blind clamour made me wise; Then was I as a child that cries, But crying, knows his father near; And what I am beheld again What is, and no man understands; And out of darkness came the hands That reach thro' nature, moulding men.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker reflects on the divine as both a source of deepest faith and greatest doubt.
- The speaker cannot find God through the external world, nature, or human reasoning alone.
- When faith weakens and doubt urges disbelief, an inner feeling resists cold reason.

prompts.L4:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: That, Our, They

outputs.L1:
That which we dare invoke to bless:  
Our dearest faith, our ghastliest doubt;  
He, They, One, All; within, without;  
The Power in darkness whom we guess.

I found Him not in world or sun,  
Or eagle’s wing, or insect’s eye;  
Nor through the questions men may try—  
The petty cobwebs we have spun.

If ever, when faith had fallen asleep,  
I heard a voice, “Believe no more,”  
And heard an ever-breaking shore  
That tumbled in the Godless deep,

A warmth within the breast would melt  
The freezing reason’s colder part;  
And, like a man in wrath, the heart  
Stood up and answered, “I have felt.”

No—like a child in doubt and fear;  
Yet that blind clamour made me wise.  
Then was I as a child that cries,  
But, crying, knows his father near.

And what I am beheld again  
What is, and no man understands;  
And out of darkness came the hands  
That reach through nature, moulding men.
outputs.L2:
What we are bold enough to call upon for blessing—  
our most cherished belief and our most terrible uncertainty;  
whether named He, They, One, or All;  
present inside us and beyond us;  
the hidden force in darkness that we only imagine—  

I did not discover Him in the earth or in the sun,  
nor in the flight of an eagle or the eye of an insect.  
I did not find Him through the questions people devise,  
those fragile little webs of thought we weave.  

If, at some time when faith had grown dormant,  
I seemed to hear a voice saying, “Trust no longer,”  
and heard the endless crash of waves  
falling into a sea without God,  
then a heat within my chest would soften  
the icy portion of reason,  
and the heart, like an angry man rising up,  
would reply, “I have known this by feeling.”  

No—not like an angry man, but like a frightened child,  
uncertain and afraid.  
Yet that confused cry taught me wisdom.  
I became like a child who weeps,  
but, even while weeping, knows his father is close.  

Then my own being once more perceived  
the reality that exists, though no human fully comprehends it;  
and from the darkness emerged the hands  
that extend through nature, shaping humankind.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents the divine as both the source of their deepest faith and the cause of their greatest doubt. God is not described as something simple or easily understood, but as a mystery that continually challenges the speaker’s mind and spirit. This tension creates an inward struggle: the speaker longs to believe, yet also feels the pressure of uncertainty.

The speaker explains that God cannot be fully discovered through the external world alone. Nature, reason, and human observation are not enough to provide complete certainty. Although the world may suggest the presence of a higher power, it does not offer undeniable proof. Human reasoning, with all its limits, cannot fully grasp the divine or resolve every question that faith raises.

Yet when faith begins to weaken and doubt encourages disbelief, something within the speaker resists. Cold logic may argue against belief, but the heart responds with a deeper emotional conviction. This inner feeling does not depend on outward evidence or rational explanation. Instead, it offers a form of certainty that comes from personal experience and spiritual intuition.

The speaker’s heart answers doubt by affirming a direct awareness of the divine. Even when the mind struggles, the soul seems to recognize God’s presence. This emotional certainty becomes stronger than abstract reasoning, suggesting that faith is not based only on proof, but also on an inward encounter with something sacred.

Finally, in moments of darkness, fear, and uncertainty, the speaker senses a guiding presence at work. This presence appears to move through nature and human life, shaping humanity with purpose and care. Though the divine may remain mysterious, the speaker feels that God is not absent. Instead, God is experienced as a hidden but powerful force, guiding both the individual soul and the larger course of human existence.
outputs.L4:
The speaker reflects on the deep and often painful struggle between faith and doubt. Rather than presenting belief in God as something simple or easily proven, the speaker shows how uncertain and fragile faith can feel when the mind begins to question. The natural world, which is often seen as evidence of divine order and beauty, does not provide complete reassurance. Human reason also fails to offer a final answer. Logic, argument, and observation may lead only to confusion, because they cannot fully explain spiritual truth or remove the darkness of uncertainty.

In this state of doubt, the speaker turns inward. Instead of searching for proof outside the self, the speaker looks to personal feeling and emotional experience. It is within the depths of the heart that a sense of God’s presence begins to emerge. This experience is not a clear intellectual proof, but it is powerful and transformative. Even when the world seems dark and the mind cannot find certainty, the soul may still feel touched by something divine. That inward feeling becomes a source of comfort and renewal.

The central insight is that faith is restored not through external evidence or rational demonstration, but through an inner awareness of God. The speaker suggests that spiritual conviction depends less on what can be seen or logically proven and more on what is deeply felt. In moments of fear, darkness, and uncertainty, the emotional experience of divine nearness gives strength to believe again. Faith, then, is not the absence of doubt, but the ability to find meaning and reassurance even within doubt. It arises from an inward sense of connection with God, a feeling that survives when reason and outward signs are insufficient.
outputs.L5:
That moment reminded us of our shared responsibility. Our choices, small or large, shape the world around us every day. They may seem simple at first, but together they create a path toward understanding, kindness, and progress.

That is why we must value our voices and use them wisely. They can encourage others, build trust, and bring people closer. Our actions matter, and they can make a difference when guided by respect and hope.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style religious poem about doubt, faith, and finding God through inner feeling rather than reason.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Hidden Witness**

I sought Thee once with lamp of mind,  
Through cloistered page and learned art;  
But evermore I failed to find  
The path that led me to Thy heart.  

The stars were cold, the books were dim,  
The preacher’s thunder passed me by;  
I heard the distant seraphim,  
Yet felt no wing descend the sky.  

Then Doubt, in garments grey and worn,  
Sat by my hearth and spake with me:  
“Behold,” he cried, “thy faith is torn;  
What God remains whom none may see?”  

I answered not; for Reason’s blade  
Had cleft my ancient hopes in twain,  
And all my prayers, once richly made,  
Fell back like echoes full of pain.  

But in the hush where sorrow kneels,  
When mortal pride has ceased to strive,  
There woke within those deeper peals  
By which the buried soul is live.  

No argument with shining crown,  
No proof from earth, nor sea, nor sun,  
But something inly breathing down  
A peace that made my spirit one.  

It was not thought that found Thee there,  
Nor wisdom’s ladder, rung by rung;  
It was the pulse beneath my prayer,  
The wordless hymn my longing sung.  

I felt Thee as the violet feels  
The secret April in the sod;  
As wounded flesh, when comfort steals,  
Knows less the balm than knows its God.  

O Lord, not in the cloud of fire,  
Nor storm that rends the mountain-stone,  
But in the trembling heart’s desire  
Thou mak’st Thy gentlest presence known.  

So let the scholars doubt and prove,  
And let the creeds in conflict roll;  
I hold Thee by the inward love  
That lights the chapel of the soul.  

And if again the night descend,  
And questions rise like mist at sea,  
Still shall my poor heart comprehend  
What reason cannot: Thou art near to me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a passage in the style of Alfred Lord Tennyson’s “In Memoriam,” using archaic diction and themes of grief, skepticism, and divine presence.
counterfactuals.output:
O Thou, who hid’st behind the veil  
Of cloud and star and mortal breath,  
I grope along the brink of death,  
And question if Thy hand prevail.

The night is deep; the winds are chill;  
Old voices perish in the rain;  
My heart, that calleth, calls in vain,  
Yet listens for an answer still.

I loved him well: the earth was fair  
When in his eyes the morning shone;  
Now every field is overgrown  
With shadows of a mute despair.

And oft I say, “If God be just,  
Why breaks He thus the tender reed?  
Why leaves He Love to ache and bleed,  
And crowns our comeliness with dust?”

Yet, while I doubt, some inward flame  
Awakes beneath the grief I bear;  
A stillness trembles through the air,  
And whispers of a hidden Name.

Not as the thunder, loud and near,  
Nor as the sun in noonday skies,  
But as a tear that purifies,  
Thy presence falls upon my fear.

So let me mourn, yet not deny;  
Let sorrow keep her sacred place;  
Perchance, beyond the bounds of space,  
The dead are living, and not die.

And if the soul, through dark and strife,  
Must pass where mortal sense is dim,  
I faintly trust it moves to Him  
Who is the Life within all life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic meditation where the speaker searches for God in nature and philosophy but ultimately discovers faith in the human heart.
counterfactuals.output:
I searched for God in the cedar’s height,  
where green spires lifted their prayers to the sky,  
and the wind moved through them like a hymn  
too old for any tongue to hold.  

I knelt beside rivers,  
watching them carry the broken light  
as if heaven had shattered  
and was flowing home in silver pieces.  
I asked the mountains, stern and silent,  
whether they had seen His face—  
but they answered only with snow,  
with patience,  
with stones remembering fire.  

Then I turned to thought,  
to the bright labyrinth of names:  
Being, First Cause, Eternal Mind,  
the unmoved center of all turning.  
I traced the geometry of angels,  
weighed proofs like coins in the palm,  
and climbed the stairways of reason  
until the air grew thin  
and every conclusion opened  
into another question.  

Still, I was hungry.  
Still, the world, though full of signs,  
did not speak plainly.  
The stars burned above me  
like distant lamps in a house  
whose door I could not find.  

At last, weary of looking upward,  
I looked across.  

There—  
in the hand that reached for mine  
without asking what I believed,  
in the mother bending over a fevered child,  
in the stranger who shared bread  
and disappeared before thanks could name him,  
in forgiveness, trembling but alive,  
in grief that made room for another’s grief—  
I felt something vast draw near.  

Not thunder.  
Not proof.  
Not a voice from beyond the clouds.  

Only the quiet astonishment  
that love could rise from dust,  
that mercy could bloom  
in the narrow soil of the human heart,  
that we, so small and wounded,  
could become windows  
for an infinite light.  

Then I understood:  
faith was not a treasure hidden  
at the far edge of the world,  
nor a theorem locked in crystal thought.  
It had been beating beside me all along,  
a pulse beneath every question,  
a flame passed palm to palm,  
God’s most secret dwelling—  
not beyond the earth,  
but within the heart  
that learns to love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a 19th-century rhymed poem with lines about “He, They, One, All,” an “ever-breaking shore,” and the heart answering doubt with “I have felt.”
counterfactuals.output:
He spake in thunder: **He** is nigh,  
**They** whispered low: His steps are fled;  
**One** watched the stars go solemn by,  
**All** bowed beside the holy dead.  

Upon an **ever-breaking shore**  
The weary waves made moan and knell;  
And Doubt cried out, “Believe no more!”  
The heart made answer, “**I have felt**.”  

“I have felt the unseen hand  
That lifts the soul when lights depart;  
I have heard, through sea and land,  
Eternity within the heart.  

Though creeds may fade and temples fall,  
Though night be deep and reason melt,  
Still He, They, One, and All in all  
Are known to love that says, ‘I felt.’”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a Tennyson-like stanza sequence exploring the conflict between cold reason and spiritual intuition, ending with unseen hands shaping mankind.
counterfactuals.output:
By midnight lamps the sages sate,  
With starry charts and balances cold;  
They weighed the dust, they measured fate,  
And found the heavens vast and old.  

“Behold,” they cried, “the law, the chain,  
The wheel that turns, the seed that dies;  
No voice is heard beyond the brain,  
No throne is builded in the skies.”  

Yet in the hush between their words  
A deeper music seemed to move,  
As when, unseen, the southward birds  
Are drawn by some remembered love.  

The heart replied, “Your lamps are bright,  
Yet not by flame alone we see;  
There walks a Presence through the night,  
Too near for proof, too far to flee.  

“You name the nerves, the dust, the breath,  
The ancient fire in clay confined;  
But who shall read through birth and death  
The secret scripture of the mind?  

“For still the mourner lifts his face,  
And still the dying whisper trust;  
And still through wrecks of time and place  
A flower arises from the dust.”  

Then Reason paused beside the sea,  
Where moon and wave were silver-blent,  
And heard, as from eternity,  
A tide beyond the element.  

“O soul,” she said, “I cannot know  
The height to which thy dreams aspire;  
Yet all my icy peaks below  
Are kindled by thy hidden fire.”  

So Faith and Thought, no more at strife,  
Went forth beneath the morning wind,  
To read in death the roots of life,  
And feel through change one Will behind—  

Till, past the veil of cloud and star,  
Past all that sense has named or spanned,  
They dimly knew what Powers there are:  
Unseen hands shaping mankind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
